verses.t: Mencius said, "Shun was born in Zhufeng, moved to Fuxia, and died in Mingtiao; he was a man of the eastern tribes. King Wen was born in Qizhou and died in Biying; he was a man of the western tribes. Their lands were more than a thousand li apart, and their ages more than a thousand years apart. Yet when they had their way and acted in the Middle Kingdom, it was like the two halves of a tally fitting together. The earlier sage and the later sage measured by one and the same standard."

When Zichan was in charge of the government of Zheng, he used his own carriage to carry people across the Zhen and the Wei. Mencius said, "He was kind, but he did not know how to govern. If the footbridges are finished in the eleventh month of the year, and the carriage bridges in the twelfth month, the people will not suffer from fording rivers. If a gentleman keeps his government fair, he may even have people cleared from his path when he goes out. How can he carry everyone across one by one? If one who governs tried to please everyone one by one, the days would not be long enough."

Mencius said to King Xuan of Qi, "When a ruler regards his ministers as his hands and feet, they regard him as their belly and heart. When a ruler regards his ministers as dogs and horses, they regard him as any man in the street. When a ruler regards his ministers as dirt and weeds, they regard him as a bandit and an enemy." The king said, "According to the rites, a minister wears mourning for a ruler he formerly served. What must a ruler do so that this mourning will be worn for him?" Mencius said, "When the minister's advice is followed and his words are heeded, so that blessings flow down to the people; when, having some reason to leave, he is escorted by the ruler's men beyond the border, and the ruler sends word ahead to the place he is going; and when, only after he has been gone three years without returning, his lands and house are taken back: this is called the threefold courtesy. If a ruler acts like this, mourning will be worn for him. Nowadays, when one is a minister, his advice is not followed and his words are not heeded, so no blessings flow down to the people. When he has some reason to leave, the ruler has him seized and bound, and also makes things as hard as possible for him in the place he is going; and on the day he leaves, his lands and house are taken back. This is what is called a bandit and an enemy. What mourning is there for a bandit and an enemy?"
Mencius said, "When scholars are put to death for no crime, great officers may leave the state. When the common people are slaughtered for no crime, scholars may move away."
Mencius said, "If the ruler is benevolent, everyone will be benevolent; if the ruler is righteous, everyone will be righteous."
Mencius said, "Rites that are not true rites, and righteousness that is not true righteousness, the great man does not practise."

Mencius said, "Those who keep to the mean nurture those who do not; those who are talented nurture those who are not. That is why people are glad to have worthy fathers and elder brothers. If those who keep to the mean abandoned those who do not, and the talented abandoned those who are not, then the distance between the worthy and the unworthy would not be an inch."
Mencius said, "Only when a man will not do certain things is he able to do great things."
Mencius said, "When a man speaks of the faults of others, what about the trouble it will bring him later?" Mencius said, "Zhongni did not go to extremes."
Mencius said, "The great man does not insist that his words be kept or that his actions be carried through; he does only what is right."
Mencius said, "The great man is one who does not lose the heart of a newborn child."
Mencius said, "Caring for one's parents while they live is not enough to count as the great thing; only seeing them off in death can count as the great thing."

Mencius said, "The gentleman goes deeply into it by the proper way because he wants to find it in himself. When he finds it in himself, he dwells in it at ease. When he dwells in it at ease, he draws on it deeply. When he draws on it deeply, he finds its source wherever he turns, to left or right. That is why the gentleman wants to find it in himself."
Mencius said, "One learns widely and explains things in detail in order to return and set out what is essential."

Mencius said, "No one has ever been able to subdue others by using goodness to subdue them. Only by using goodness to nurture others can one win over the world. There has never been one who became king without the world submitting to him in its heart."
Mencius said, "Words without substance are ill-omened. The substance of what is truly ill-omened falls on those who hide away worthy men."

Xuzi said, "Zhongni often praised water, saying, 'Water! Water!' What did he find in water?" Mencius said, "A spring with a source wells up, never ceasing day or night. It fills up every hollow and then moves on, until it reaches the four seas. What has a source is like this, and that is what he found in it. If there is no source, then in the seventh and eighth months, when the rains gather, the ditches and channels all fill up, but one can stand and wait for them to dry out again. So the gentleman is ashamed of a reputation that goes beyond the reality."

Mencius said, "That by which man differs from the birds and beasts is very slight. The common people cast it away; the gentleman preserves it. Shun understood the nature of things and saw clearly into human relations. He acted from benevolence and righteousness; he did not merely practise benevolence and righteousness."

Mencius said, "Yu hated fine wine and loved good words. Tang held to the middle way and raised up worthy men without regard to their background. King Wen looked on the people as if they were wounded, and he gazed toward the Way as if he had not yet seen it. King Wu did not slight those near at hand nor forget those far away. The Duke of Zhou thought to combine [the virtues of] the three kings and to carry out the four kinds of their deeds. When there was something that did not fit, he looked up and pondered it, day and night. If he was fortunate enough to find the answer, he sat waiting for the dawn [to put it into practice]."

Mencius said, "When the traces of the true kings disappeared, the Odes ceased to be made. When the Odes ceased, the Spring and Autumn was written. The Sheng of Jin, the Taowu of Chu and the Spring and Autumn of Lu are all of one kind. Their subject is Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin, and their style is that of the court historians. Confucius said, 'As for its meaning, I have ventured to take that upon myself.'"

Mencius said, "The influence of a gentleman comes to an end after five generations, and so does the influence of a small man. I was not able to be a disciple of Confucius, but I have cultivated myself through others [who learned from him]."

Mencius said, "When one may take something or may leave it, taking it does harm to integrity. When one may give something or may not give it, giving it does harm to kindness. When one may die or may not die, dying does harm to courage."

Pang Meng learned archery from Yi. When he had learned all of Yi's art, he thought that in all the world only Yi was better than himself, so he killed Yi. Mencius said, "Yi too was at fault in this. Gongming Yi said, 'It seems he was not at fault.' He only meant that his fault was slight; how could he be without fault? The people of Zheng sent Zizhuo Ruzi to invade Wey, and Wey sent Yugong Zhisi to pursue him. Zizhuo Ruzi said, 'Today my illness has come on and I cannot hold my bow. I am a dead man!' He asked his driver, 'Who is pursuing me?' The driver said, 'Yugong Zhisi.' He said, 'Then I shall live.' The driver said, 'Yugong Zhisi is the best archer in Wey. Why do you say, "I shall live"?' He said, 'Yugong Zhisi learned archery from Yingong Zhituo, and Yingong Zhituo learned archery from me. Yingong Zhituo is an upright man, and the friends he chooses are sure to be upright.' When Yugong Zhisi came up, he said, 'Master, why are you not holding your bow?' Zizhuo Ruzi said, 'Today my illness has come on and I cannot hold my bow.' Yugong Zhisi said, 'I learned archery from Yingong Zhituo, and Yingong Zhituo learned archery from you, Master. I cannot bear to use your own art to harm you. Even so, today's business is my ruler's business, and I dare not neglect it.' He drew out his arrows, knocked them against the wheel to break off their metal heads, shot four of them, and then turned back."

Mencius said, "If Xizi [the beauty] were covered with filth, everyone would hold their noses as they passed her. But even an ugly man, if he fasts and purifies himself and bathes, may offer sacrifice to God on High."

Mencius said, "When people in the world talk about human nature, they simply follow what has already happened, and what has already happened is grounded in what comes naturally. What one dislikes about the clever is that they force things. If the clever acted as Yu did when he guided the waters, there would be nothing to dislike in their cleverness. When Yu guided the waters, he guided them along the way that gave him no trouble. If the clever also went the way that gives no trouble, their cleverness would be great indeed. Heaven is high and the stars are far away, but if we look into what has already happened, we can work out the solstices for a thousand years without leaving our seats."

When Gonghangzi was mourning his son, the Commander of the Right went to offer condolences. As he entered the gate, some came forward to speak with him, and others went over to where he was seated to speak with him. Mencius did not speak with him, and the Commander of the Right was displeased, saying, "All the gentlemen spoke with me, Huan; only Mencius did not speak with me. He is slighting me." Mencius heard of this and said, "According to the rites, at court one does not cross over to another's place to speak with him, nor go beyond the steps to bow to him. I wished to observe the rites, and Ziao thinks I was slighting him. Is that not strange?"

Mencius said, "What makes the gentleman different from others is what he keeps in his heart. The gentleman keeps benevolence in his heart and keeps the rites in his heart. The benevolent man loves others; the man of the rites respects others. One who loves others is always loved by them; one who respects others is always respected by them. Suppose there is a man who treats me with harshness and unreason. The gentleman will surely turn back on himself and say, 'I must have been lacking in benevolence, I must have been lacking in courtesy. How else could such a thing have happened to me?' If he turns back on himself and finds he has been benevolent and courteous, and the man is still harsh and unreasonable, the gentleman will surely turn back on himself and say, 'I must not have done my best for him.' If he turns back on himself and finds he has done his best, and the man is still harsh and unreasonable, the gentleman will say, 'This is simply a reckless man. Such a man is no different from a beast, and why should I trouble myself over a beast?' Therefore the gentleman has a lifelong concern but no passing worries. His concern is this: 'Shun was a man, and I too am a man. Shun became a model for the world that could be handed down to later ages, while I am still only an ordinary villager.' This is something to be concerned about. What is to be done about it? Simply to be like Shun. As for passing worries, the gentleman has none. He does nothing that is not benevolent and nothing that is not according to the rites. Even if some passing trouble should come, the gentleman does not worry about it."

Yu and Ji lived in a time of peace; three times they passed their own doors without going in, and Confucius praised them as worthy. Master Yan lived in a time of disorder and dwelt in a mean alley, with a single basket of rice and a single gourd of water. Others could not have borne such hardship, but Master Yan did not let it change his joy, and Confucius praised him as worthy. Mencius said, "Yu, Ji and Yan Hui followed the same Way. Yu thought that if anyone in the world was drowning, it was as if he himself had drowned him. Ji thought that if anyone in the world was hungry, it was as if he himself had made him hungry. That is why they acted with such urgency. If Yu, Ji and Master Yan had changed places, each would have done as the others did. Now if people in your own household are fighting, you may go to stop them even with your hair loose and your cap-strings untied. But if people in your neighbourhood are fighting and you rush out to stop them with your hair loose and your cap-strings untied, you are mistaken; it would be right to shut your door."

Gongduzi said, "Kuang Zhang is called unfilial by everyone in the state. Yet you go about with him, Master, and even treat him with courtesy. May I ask why?" Mencius said, "There are five things the world commonly calls unfilial. To be lazy with one's four limbs and not see to the support of one's parents is the first. To gamble and play chess and love drinking, and not see to the support of one's parents, is the second. To love goods and money and favour one's wife and children, and not see to the support of one's parents, is the third. To follow the desires of one's ears and eyes and so bring disgrace on one's parents is the fourth. To love daring and quarrelling and so put one's parents in danger is the fifth. Is Zhangzi guilty of any one of these? Zhangzi and his father reproached each other for not doing good, and so they fell out. Reproaching each other for not doing good is the way of friends; between father and son, it is the greatest injury to the love between them. Did Zhangzi not want to have a wife and children around him? But because he had offended his father and could not come near him, he sent away his wife and drove off his son, and does without their care for the rest of his life. He reasoned in his heart that if he did not do this, his crime would be greater still. That is what Zhangzi is."

When Zengzi was living in Wucheng, there was a raid from Yue. Someone said, "The raiders are coming. Why not leave?" Zengzi said, "Do not let anyone lodge in my house and damage the trees and plants." When the raiders withdrew, he sent word: "Repair my walls and house; I am coming back." When the raiders withdrew, Zengzi came back. Those around him said, "The master has been treated here with such loyalty and respect. Yet when the raiders came he was the first to leave, setting an example for the people, and when they withdrew he came back. That seems hardly right." Shenyou Xing said, "This is not something you understand. Once, when the Shenyou family suffered trouble from a man called Fuchu, the master had seventy followers with him, and none of them took part [in the fighting]." When Zisi was living in Wey, there was a raid from Qi. Someone said, "The raiders are coming. Why not leave?" Zisi said, "If I leave, who will help the ruler defend the state?" Mencius said, "Zengzi and Zisi followed the same Way. Zengzi was a teacher, in the position of a father or elder brother; Zisi was a subject, in a humble position. If Zengzi and Zisi had changed places, each would have done as the other did."

Chuzi said, "The king sent someone to spy on you, Master, to see whether you really are different from other men." Mencius said, "How would I be different from other men? Even Yao and Shun were the same as other men."

There was a man of Qi who lived with a wife and a concubine. Whenever their husband went out, he would come back stuffed with wine and meat. When his wife asked him whom he had been eating and drinking with, they were all rich and noble people. His wife said to the concubine, "Whenever our husband goes out, he comes back stuffed with wine and meat, and when I ask whom he has been eating and drinking with, they are all rich and noble people. Yet no one of distinction has ever come here. I am going to watch where our husband goes." She got up early and secretly followed her husband wherever he went. In the whole city no one stopped to talk with him. At last he went to the graves outside the eastern wall, where people were offering sacrifices, and begged their leftovers. When that was not enough, he looked around and went on to others. This was how he got himself stuffed. His wife went home and told the concubine, "Our husband is the one we look up to and depend on for the rest of our lives, and now he is like this!" She and the concubine reviled their husband and wept together in the courtyard. The husband, knowing nothing of this, came swaggering in from outside and put on airs before his wife and concubine. In the eyes of the gentleman, few indeed of those who seek riches, honour, profit and advancement do so by means of which their wives and concubines would not be ashamed, and over which they would not weep together.
